caption:
FORMER OPENAI CTO MIRA MURATI JUST RELEASED AN AI MODEL THAT CAN BUILD GAMES ON A LAPTOP WITHOUT INTERNET. 🤯

And the technology behind it could change how AI models are designed.

On November 20, Mira Murati's startup, Thinking Machines Lab, introduced Inkling 2 Mini, a powerful open-weights AI model that can run locally on a laptop.

The team even tested it on a MacBook Pro in airplane mode, where it built a playable flight simulator in just a few minutes.

But the real breakthrough is how this AI model thinks.

Instead of processing information through its neural network layers just once, Inkling 2 Mini repeatedly runs its middle layers to perform additional internal computation.

Here's what makes it interesting:

•26.4 Billion Parameters: Only 3.4 billion are active per token, keeping the model relatively efficient.

•3 Reasoning Loops: Its middle transformer layers run three times, allowing more internal computation before generating output.

•Runs Offline: The model can operate locally on compatible laptops with at least 32GB RAM.

•Impressive Coding Performance: It scored 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, leading open-weights models under 100 billion parameters in the company's published comparison.

•Open Weights: Developers can download the model from Hugging Face and run it using tools like Ollama.

There's also an interesting trade-off. More internal reasoning can make AI harder to monitor because not every computation appears in its written reasoning.

The bigger story isn't just another AI model launch.

It's the possibility of powerful AI agents running directly on personal computers, without depending on cloud servers.

caption:
AI JUST COMPRESSED 1 GB OF WIKIPEDIA INTO ONLY 105 MB WITHOUT LOSING A SINGLE LETTER🤖

And the technology behind this breakthrough is seriously impressive.

A new open-source AI compression system called tufazip, developed by Tommy He at Tufa Labs, has demonstrated how neural networks can compress enormous amounts of text while preserving every single byte of the original data.

The system compressed a 1-billion-byte Wikipedia dataset into just 105.39 MB, achieving nearly 90% compression without losing any information.

Here's what makes this fascinating:

•1 GB to 105 MB: The original Wikipedia text was reduced to roughly one-tenth of its size.

•100% Lossless: Every character can be reconstructed exactly as it appeared in the original file.

•163 Million Parameters: A 12-layer Transformer learns patterns in text to predict what comes next.

•AI-Powered Compression: Instead of simply finding repeated text like traditional ZIP compression, the model uses probabilities to encode information efficiently.

•Open Source: The project's code is available on GitHub for researchers and developers.

But there's a massive catch.

The experiment required two NVIDIA B200 GPUs and approximately 7.3 days of computation just to compress the dataset. Decompression also takes several days.

That makes tufazip a research breakthrough rather than a practical replacement for ZIP today.

Still, it achieved second place on a long-running text compression benchmark at the time of submission.

The bigger idea is fascinating: The better AI becomes at predicting information, the better it can potentially become at compressing it.

AI isn't just generating information anymore. It's learning how to store it more efficiently.
